newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: INTERVIEW - SAS eyeing Baltic routes, not airlines.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - SAS eyeing Baltic routes, not airlines.

text.p: Scandinavian airline SAS, which owns nearly one third of Latvian airline Air Baltic, said it was satisfied with its cooperation with the Baltic carrier but stopped short of saying it was eyeing other Baltic airlines.
Jan Lundborg, head of eastern Europe and Baltic routes for SAS, told Reuters in an interview SAS could be interested in Lithuanian Airlines but said it was not in talks with the company.
Last week Lithuania said it planned to sell off more than 50 percent of the Vilnius-based air carrier, but that half of the national carrier would remain with Lithuanian investors.
"We don't know what we want to do today. We haven't had any discussions with Lithuanian Airlines," Lundborg said.
"We'll see what happens," he said.
Latvia's Air Baltic, formed from Latvia's old state airline, is 51 percent owned by the Latvian government and 29 percent owned by SAS. Swedfund and the Danish Investment Fund also own stakes.
SAS at one time had been interested in a 66 percent stake in Estonia's national carrier, Estonian Air, but was outbid by Danish airline Maersk Air A/S.
After a rough start, Lundborg said SAS would start to enjoy more synergies from the meshing of its own traffic programmes with that of Air Baltic. The two airlines now have code sharing.
"It was tough in the beginning but now it's starting to show a better result," Lundborg said.
"We're satisfied because we have actually tied our traffic programmes together.
"We have a code share product together with them...for the customer it means there's quite a lot to chose from when you want to travel between Scandinavia and Riga," he said.
Lundborg said the next step was to coordinate travel of Air Baltic passengers through Copenhagen and Stockholm and onto other SAS destinations.
"It takes time of course to get that into place because of slot restrictions and so on but that is now getting into place and I feel it's working pretty good."
It was unlikely that SAS would try to increase its stake in Air Baltic, Lundborg said.
"I don't think SAS wants to own companies to a larger extent. It's controlled by the Latvian side by 51 percent and that's the intention. This is the national carrier of Latvia," he said.
He said the intention was to build up the national carrier and SAS' relationship with Air Baltic would probably be like that with Thai Airways.
"What we have done there is tried to help them with the know-how and within reasonable time the SAS people invloved will no longer work and it will be taken over by Latvia."
SAS currently flies from Copenhagen and Stockholm to all three Baltic capitals.
Since November it has been operating three regular flights per week between Stockholm and Vilnius, adding to its flights to the Lithuanian capital from Copenhagen.
A dispute with Estonian air authorities forced SAS to cut flights between Tallinn and Copenhagen to ten but it was able to increase flights between Stockholm and Tallinn.
"We intend for the winter traffic from November 1997 to go back to a daily operation from Stockholm to Tallinn and a double daily operation from Copenhagen to Tallinn," Lundborg said.
SAS would like to increase its flights between Stockholm and Vilnius but would wait until cabin factors picked up, he said.
"We have a cabin factor of about 30-35 percent. It's not the best, but then it's also the winter period," Lundborg said.
